title: Grouped summaries with missing values
explanation: Real summaries hit real problems: missing values, and groups too small to trust. This lesson uses `deliveries`, where 3 tips are missing (NA), and shows how to handle both.

tasks.prompt: For each restaurant, count the orders and find the average delivery minutes, rounded to 1 decimal, in columns orders and avg_minutes.
hints: result <- deliveries |> group_by(restaurant) |> summarize(orders = n(), avg_minutes = round(mean(minutes), 1))
tasks.answer: result <- deliveries |> group_by(restaurant) |> summarize(orders = n(), avg_minutes = round(mean(minutes), 1))

tasks.teach: Remember from Level 1: one NA makes mean() give NA. **na.rm = TRUE** skips them, group by group.
tasks.prompt: Find each restaurant's average tip, rounded to 2 decimals, in a column called avg_tip. Some tips are NA, so skip them with na.rm = TRUE.
hints: Without na.rm = TRUE, restaurants with a missing tip would show NA.
result <- deliveries |> group_by(restaurant) |> summarize(avg_tip = round(mean(tip, na.rm = TRUE), 2))
tasks.answer: result <- deliveries |> group_by(restaurant) |> summarize(avg_tip = round(mean(tip, na.rm = TRUE), 2))

tasks.teach: filter() **after** summarize() filters the groups, like HAVING in SQL.
tasks.prompt: Last one: averages from 1 or 2 orders aren't reliable. Repeat the first summary, then keep only restaurants with at least 3 orders, using filter() after summarize().
hints: filter() works on the summary table too.
tasks.answer: result <- deliveries |> group_by(restaurant) |> summarize(orders = n(), avg_minutes = round(mean(minutes), 1)) |> filter(orders >= 3)

recap: Use na.rm = TRUE inside summaries when there are NAs. filter() after summarize() keeps only the groups you trust, like SQL's HAVING.
